utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Just in order to raise a point that was broached tomorrow [as interpreted] we talked about those three documents, MFI 00041, 00042, and 00043, the three documents that were marked for identification, those that I had tendered. Before we started today I spoke to my learned friend from the OTP and these are in relation to the ones that were admitted yesterday. I don't think there is any opposition to my motion to have these admitted. So may the Chamber please rule on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That is the position, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, apparently they are linked. If they are linked, we cannot oppose that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Those three documents will now be received in evidence. While that is occurring, good morning, Doctor, welcome back.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Given the lapse of time I'd ask you to take the affirmation again. If you'd stand and read it from the card, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, MFI 41, MFI 42, and MFI 43, from now on will be Exhibit Number 41, exhibit number 42 and Exhibit Number 43.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Through. Yes, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would be delighted to assist. Unfortunately it it's not my turn. I think it's cross-examination on behalf of Mr. Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I thought there may have been some additional issue, but if there is not, I move straight across. Always ready to give you a little nibble at the cherry, Mr. Moore. Now we go straight to Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to all.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Njavro. Let me introduce myself, I am Bulatovic, one of Mr. Sljivancanin's Defence counsel. We both speak the same language, I don't think we'll be having any communication problems, but it is for the benefit of the interpreters that I would like to ask you to please make a pause between my question and your answer every time in order to allow for the interpreters to do their job properly, and so that we may have an accurate transcript. At the outset there is a date that I'd like to bring up. It's something you mentioned in your previous testimony in relation to a specific event. If you remember, I'm talking about the October evacuation of wounded persons from Vukovar Hospital. Do you remember that evacuation, sir?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember when exactly that occurred?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 19th of October, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember how many wounded were evacuated on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would be hard put to give you the exact figure, but it may have been between 107 and 112 wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember who was at the head of that convoy, or rather who escorted the convoy all the way to the Vukovar Hospital?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the Medecins sans Frontieres. They escorted the convoy up to the hospital first, and then away from the hospital. That's what the organisation is called.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Does the name of Robert Michel ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Not that it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: So the MSF were at the head of that convoy, they were the organisers. Do you know if there was anybody providing escort for the convoy, any military forces. If so, just whose?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure about there being any military forces escorting the convoy up to the hospital. However, on the convoy's way out of the hospital, and as they were crossing a certain section of town, and then on to Luzac, and further off across the fields, once they passed Luzac, which was an area under JNA command and it was also under the control of paramilitary forces, there was a gentleman who told me something about this, but I don't remember his rank, I believe the name was Zvonko Mihajlovic, possibly Markovic. He told me that he was born in the same town or was a former schoolmate of Mr. Mrksic and pursuant to General Raseta's orders he was placed in charge of escorting that convoy. He told me so in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember if the convoy crossed Bogdanovci on its way?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: They headed out that way. It had been agreed, at least as far as I know that they would be taking the Bogdanovci route, then to Marinci, Zidine, and Nustar; however, they turned off into a field just before they reached Bogdanovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who was holding Bogdanovci at the time?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time it was still the ZNG.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know if the area around Bogdanovci was booby-trapped, were there any mines around that area?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did hear something about certain sections of that area being booby-trapped. I knew there was a real possibility of hitting a mine at some point, but I didn't know the precise locations of those mines.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Those are military matters, I will not tire you with these issues. There's something else I want to know. Do you know who was in charge of selecting the wounded who were supposed to leave on that convoy?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe Mr. Borovic asked me that and I answered that question. The hospital's doctors asked about the seriously wounded, or rather they spoke to them and they asked each and every one of them in turn if they wanted the MSF to take them to other health institutions where they would receive better treatment. Dr. Bosanac did likewise, and so did I, and so did a number of other doctors. There was a whole group of hospital doctors who took part in this decision-making process. And each patient was given a chance to say whether they would like to proceed with the MSF or stay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You were speaking about this on cross-examination when prompted by Mr. Borovic, but there's something that remains unclear. Do you remember a soldier by the name of Ivan Zivkovic?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is precisely something that I would like to add something about. I know Ivan Zivkovic, he was a soldier at the time, he still lives in Vinkovci, he had sustained a number of serious injuries and this should be easy enough to verify. I did answer a number of questions from Mr. Borovic about this person. There might be other people called Ivan Zivkovic. As you know that is a very common name, both in Croatia and in Serbia, as well as in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Throughout the former Yugoslavia, I guess you might say, Zivkovic was a very common surname.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What I don't quite understand about the selection process, how many seriously wounded were there at the Vukovar Hospital back in October 1991?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: In mid-October, or thereabouts, there was talk that the convoy would be arriving earlier, and then there were all the problems that we have spoken about, and then suddenly it was the 19th and at this point I think there may have been about 400, up to 450 wounded there, but I would be hard put to give you is a more accurate figure than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What I want to know now is about selecting these 104, up to 112, you said. Did that depend on the doctor's opinion or on the patient's personal desires? Were they free to choose where they would go?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It very much depended on the condition of those patients. Bearing in mind the horror that those people had been through, and the horror that they were experiencing on a daily basis, it was only natural that all of them would want to get out as soon as possible to avoid all these horrific experiences, but those who were eventually selected were the ones requiring urgent medical assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Was there any one doctor who had the say, as it were, in deciding which of patients would go?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very difficult to say that sort of thing now. I don't think there were any major differences of opinion in terms of professional views. This was not about the doctors' internal hierarchy, that wasn't what the decision-making process was based on, the principal criterion was the seriousness, as it were, of injuries, and the possibility of future complications to the patient's health.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: About the 19th of October convoy, were you in touch with members of the ECMM who were on that convoy?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I talked to someone who said he was in charge of the MSF convoy. I don't remember the man's name. I do know that he offered me an insignificant amount of medicine and medical equipment. I don't remember what my answer was at the time, but what's certain is that by doing what they did and by taking away a large number of wounded, they managed to save a whole lot of lives. Whenever I can I meet up with those people, just because I like to thank them for the humanitarian action that they took at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember if there was anybody on behalf of the JNA there together with the European monitors? I mean on that convoy.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say. We were all busy getting our patients ready to go. You will understand that there was to be an evacuation and there was some people who had sustained serious wounds. These people had to be prepared and we were busy doing just that. I can't say who else was there, the people you're asking about, but what I can tell you is that we were extremely busy getting the patients ready to go, otherwise the evacuation itself would have been jeopardised.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Njavro. Let us move on to the 18th of November 1991, now. You've spoken a great deal about that already and you testified that on the 18th of November, 1991, in the early afternoon, a military vehicle arrived in front of the hospital; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: One, or possibly two vehicles. However, a lot of time has elapsed, and that affects your memory. I do think there were two military APCs, though. Two, not one.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Please try to think back. Was it one or two?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two. I would settle for two.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did they both arrive at the same time or was there a time lag between their respective arrivals?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't quite remember, I did see two at the time. I'm not sure if there was a time lag. Whether they arrived at different times, I can't be certain about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: The APCs disgorged a number of JNA officers, right?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please just wait until I finish my question and then proceed with your answer, sir? Who was the first officer you spoke to?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The APC disgorged two officers. One of them was a captain by rank, and the other was a major.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Which of these two did you first speak to; do you remember that, sir?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was neither of those. I can't quite remember, but one of the officers said that we should all go into the hospital and not go anywhere else. This was contrary to what we had been told earlier on. We had been told that no soldiers would be entering the hospital of the they said we'd be picked up and that all medical staff would be evacuated.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: We're talking about the 18th of November, right, 1991? You say that this was contrary to what you had been told earlier on, what I want to know is what exactly were you told earlier on, and by who?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned on the 18th, if my memory still serves me well, I think Dr. Bosanac told me that she had been talking that Mr. Mrksic on the phone, what was being said is that the hospital would be evacuated and that she needn't worry. He had said that those who would be found at the hospital would be allowed to -- those who were found at the hospital would be allowed to leave the hospital. On the other hand, she was also in touch with Zagreb, she spoke to the European monitors, and I think also somebody from the Croatian government, and was told that there would be an agreement with the JNA to have the hospital evacuated.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: They were saying that there would be an agreement, which probably implies that there was no agreement in place at the time they spoke, right?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very difficult for me to say. It was said that there was an agreement already that had been signed but I never saw this agreement. However, it was also said that General Raseta, the international monitors, the International Committee of the Red Cross and representatives of the Croatia government had agreed the terms I just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You say that on the 18th you saw Mr. Sljivancanin outside the Vukovar Hospital, right?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can you say what time it was?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Early in the afternoon; 1.00, 2.00 p.m.. Difficult to say. It was in the early afternoon on that day though.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You say it was at the same time that you laid eyes on the ICRC man, Mr. Borsinger, right?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember if Mr. Borsinger arrived in his own vehicle or did he perhaps arrive with one of these officers?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a great turmoil, and the stress levels were high for all of us. Under those conditions you could hardly have expected me to notice how Mr. Borsinger arrived, in what sort of vehicle, or for that matter whether he arrived with someone else on his own.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know Mr. Borsinger from earlier on, did you meet at the negotiations or was this the first time you met him?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't quite remember whether I knew him from before. What is certain is that I saw him at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You say that at this point an argument or an altercation erupted between Mr. Borsinger and Mr. Sljivancanin, right?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: How far was that from where you were standing, and can you please describe the exact place where this occurred? In the hospital, outside the hospital?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Outside the hospital. We can go there together, if you like, and I can point the spot out to you, if that's what it takes. That would be no problem at all for me. I think my distance from them was about five or six metres. It's difficult to be more accurate than this, give or take a metre or two. Five or six metres. But I could clearly overhear their conversation, since their voices were both raised.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I'll ask you about the topic of their conversation later on, but what I want to know is which entrance, which hospital entrance while you were away, we've been looking at a great deal of photographs of the hospital building and we do have a general idea of its layout. We do know there is such a thing as the main entrance, we know about the emergency entrance so was this outside the main entrance or the emergency ward?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The main entrance and the emergency ward entrance was one and the same. It was the same door. The reception was there, a janitor was there. There was a sliding door, and this was the main door, the main entrance to the hospital, mostly used by the hospital's personnel. So that's what I define as the main entrance.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Njavro, please don't hold this against me, but we have seen a great deal of photographs here, there is such a thing as an emergency ward entrance. It's in some sort of a tunnel, or rather it's a roofed-over area. There's some sort of a roof covering the area. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to think, I'm trying to remember what it might be you're referring to. But if I might mention something, there's Gunduliceva Street, there's an entrance right there and this is when you approach Vukovar from Osijek. That might be a reference point for you. There was another principal entrance if you like and that was the one facing Ivo Lola Ribar Street. And this is when one approached from Sid or Ilok, from that general direction, and this was the main entrance to the hospital. And this is where you had guards, or rather there was a janitor who checked people on the way in. But you shouldn't confuse this one and the main entrance to the hospital building.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can we have document 170, photograph number 6 placed on our screen? I think we are compelled to go through this exercise.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you see the photograph?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: We can see both entrances on this photograph; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher, would you please use the special pen that we have, we normally call it a magic pen. And would you please mark the location where this conversation took place on the 18th, between 1300 and 1400 hours, the conversation between Mr. Sljivancanin and Mr. Borsinger?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm pointing now to the main entrance. You can see where the reception area was, where the doorman or the janitor was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Njavro, let's try to do it this way: Can you put number 1 where the main entrance into the hospital is?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm doing that right now. [Marks]. "1". I don't know if this is visible. Can you see it?

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Now please put number 2 where the entrance, the main entrance into the building is located.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: And now mark with number 3 the emergency entrance. I believe it's to the right. I don't wish to confuse you.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, let me make a distinction. Do you have in mind the emergency services itself, or just the emergency surgery?

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: The emergency surgery.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Shall I put number 3 there?

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Now, mark with number 4 the location where Mr. Borsinger and Mr. Sljivancanin talked on the 18th of November between 1.00 and 2.00 p.m.?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's impossible to do that because that area is not shown on the photograph because the tree, the tree here covers the entrance, and then there is another area and a street parallel to Ivo Lola Ribar Street, and it is at the end of that entrance that the conversation took place. However, that location is not shown on the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Then would you please indicate with an arrow the direction where that is located and mark it with number 4?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: And how far were you from there? Would you please mark your location with number 5?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks] Well, I hope this is visible enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: It is. And how far were you from that location?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have said, six to eight metres. I told you that I wasn't really good with estimating distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I want to tender this marked photograph into evidence, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be Exhibit Number 349.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Let us continue analysing this conversation. Were any other medical staff present when this conversation took place?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: There must have been other people present, but I was focused on what was going on and what was going to happen to us. Now, as to other medical personnel, whether they were there and if so, who, I can't say anything about that. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Was Mr. Borsinger on his own, or were there any other ICRC representatives there?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only remember Mr. Borsinger. I can't say that I saw anybody else there. However, it's possible that they were there. I only saw Mr. Borsinger, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see whether Mr. Sljivancanin was accompanied by any other JNA officers or was he alone?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible. As I've told you, the conditions were such for all of us, and this was after a long, exhausting period, therefore, I remember, and I paid attention only to the altercation itself, not to who else was present there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you heard the conversation between Mr. Borsinger and Mr. Sljivancanin, we can call it an argument, an altercation, whichever way you like it. Do you remember whether, in that conversation, Mr. Sljivancanin told Mr. Borsinger that during the previous night some young JNA soldiers were killed?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember hearing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that in that conversation Mr. Sljivancanin told Mr. Borsinger that if he wasn't interested in that, then he wasn't welcome where he was at the time?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already told you what I remember hearing, things that I remembered. I described that to the Trial Chamber. Now, as to whether there were any other exchanges, it is possible. I do not exclude that possibility, but I told you what I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Njavro, a witness who gave evidence here told us that in the course of 1992 and onwards Mr. Sljivancanin was frequently shown on TV programmes in Croatia. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: For sure there were programmes and there will be programmes about various topics, other topics, also involving Vukovar. Therefore, I'm not the kind of a person who bases his opinions based on what he sees or hears on television. I described to the Trial Chamber what my recollections were.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Njavro, let me interrupt you. My question was very brief. Were these programmes shown on Croatian television?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: This conversation between Borsinger and Sljivancanin, the one that you described to us, was it broadcast on television?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible but I don't remember specifically these programmes. It's possible that this was shown as well. You know yourself that the television followed every step that was taken there. They recorded it on cameras. Mostly Serbian television, and then other TV stations got that material, you know that there is an exchange of material between TV stations, therefore it is possible that other TV channels broadcast that material as well. I told you what I had heard. Now, whether there were any other exchanges, I don't know. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: Do you remember that the conversation between Borsinger and Sljivancanin was broadcast on television at any point in time, and did that affect your recollection on the conversation that took place, as you say, on the 18th of November?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think that that was necessary for me. Those are the words that I will remember for the rest of my life. I returned back to the basement. Panic ensued. People were overtaken by fear that something evil was going to happen. And this is why these words became engraved in my mind. It doesn't matter whether later on that was shown on television or not. My memory remained intact.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: That's not what I was trying to suggest.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps it was shown on television at the time. It was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You say that you went to the basement after this. Do you know what Mr. Borsinger and Sljivancanin did then?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see that. They left, Mr. Borsinger and Mr. Sljivancanin. I don't remember seeing them later.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Another brief question concerning that. How long did this go on for, was it half an hour, an hour, this conversation?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The conversation, the bit that I eye-witnessed lasted not more than five minutes, perhaps. Because after that an order was issued that all of us had to go into the hospital, and I did as I was ordered. I went back into the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Do you know who Marin Vidic, Bili, is?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You said that Marin Vidic, Bili, came to the hospital on the 18th of November, 1991. I'd like to know whether you know when exactly he came, and why.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you why he came. I can't even tell you what time it was when he came to the hospital. However, Marin Vidic, Bili, as the government commissioner in charge of the city used to come to the hospital and most often he would contact Dr. Bosanac as the hospital director.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did he come on his own on the 18th of November or with someone?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Since you were in the hospital throughout that period, do you know anything about where Mr. Vidic had his accommodation?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that, but as what I do remember, if we are now referring to the 18th.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the 18th.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember where he had accommodation. I don't know where he spent the night, if he did at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether Mr. Vidic, on the 18th of November, perhaps was present when this conversation of Mr. Sljivancanin took place and whether he was outside of the hospital on the 18th?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Dr. Bosanac came, and she said that she had contact with the ICRC, and that they would come to the hospital and take over the hospital and that we were to come outside to meet the representatives of the ICRC. However, it wasn't them who arrived, but rather APCs arrived, so the two of them went back and I think that they told me this later, but I don't remember quite clearly, that they went out to see why the ICRC representatives weren't there. So I remained on the spot that I told you, and that I marked with the magic pen.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: So it seems that you, Vesna Bosanac, Marin Vidic, came out together?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: ICRC did not appear?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Two APCs arrived?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Am I concluding right, then, that after the two APCs arrived Vesna Bosanac and Mr. Vidic went to look for the ICRC representatives?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. They came back because I think that they talked to Colonel Mrksic, and that supposedly he was also informed about this. Based on the telephone contact with Zagreb they learned that the ICRC representatives would arrive in order to take over the hospital, and so that the hospital could be evacuated. Since -- or rather when the APCs arrived, and not the ICRC representatives, I was told later that they went to see how come the ICRC representatives did not come and why was it that the army was there, or the troops who were then entering the hospital compound, even though it was said that they wouldn't do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. On the 18th you went back into the basement and when did you see Mrs. Bosanac again?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that same day, the 18th, but in the evening. I don't know whether -- or where she went or whether she spent the night at the hospital, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: On the 18th, in the evening, when you met with Mrs. Bosanac, did you discuss with her what had happened between the ICRC representative and Mr. Sljivancanin? Did you inform her that the ICRC representatives were outside of the hospital and what type of a clash occurred?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that Mrs. Bosanac, on the 18th, had already received a fax from Belgrade -- from Zagreb about the agreement that had been signed between the JNA and international observers and the Croatian government about the evacuation of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Njavro, I apologise for interrupting you. My question had a different aim, and let me rephrase it briefly. Did you, on the 18th, speak to Mrs. Bosanac about this, did you tell her that a representative of the ICRC was, on the 18th of November, outside of the Vukovar Hospital?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you perhaps talk to her? Did you tell her what sort of a misunderstanding or altercation had occurred between Mr. Sljivancanin and Mr. Borsinger?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly how our conversation proceeded. I can't say with certainty whether I told her all of these things. I stand by my previous statement, namely when I said that at the time her main worry was to have the hospital evacuated. She wasn't worrying about listening to me talking about what I'd heard being said outside the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: But you said a while ago, Mr. Njavro, that you were scared and that you realised this wouldn't work. Why didn't you convey this concern of yours to the hospital director once you had realised what was going on?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm just that sort of a person. Sometimes I tend to hide my fears. I tend not to express my fears, not to let them show. Also, in my work as a surgeon I had to deal with my own fears silently and keep them to myself. It became a part of my very person. I developed a habit of keeping these experiences to myself, and holding my fears back. But, frankly, I can't remember whether I told her or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: On the 18th of November, Mr. Njavro, did anything happen that struck you as more important than this, something that directly affected your own fate, the safety of your patients, or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've answered already a number of questions to this effect, both by the Defence and by the OTP. I told you that the hospital was in the grip of great fear. First the JNA arrived, and then the paramilitaries arrived. I told you what started happening when night fell. I have said a lot of things before this Chamber about what happened, and I have nothing to add.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: On that day, the 18th of November, Marin Vidic, Bili, Croatia's government commissioner was in the hospital, or that's what you said. Did you tell hem anything about your concerns and anything that seemed to be not in keeping with the agreement that had been reached?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Marin Vidic was a different kind of person altogether. I don't remember telling him about it, but again I can't be certain. Since I hadn't told Dr. Bosanac, I didn't think it would be necessary for me to bring this up with Marin Vidic, Bili.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you at least try to track him down, given his position at the time? Just in order to tell him that the army had arrived, contrary to the terms of the agreement that had been reached, that there was an argument between the army and the ICRC, that both you and your patients were jeopardised by this situation? He was, after all, there on behalf of Croatia's government, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think Dr. Bosanac also went to Negoslavci later on. But I think they were in charge of that, in as far as it was possible to take charge of anything at all in those circumstances I suppose I needn't even tell you about all the panic that arose, and the fear felt by everyone in the hospital. Just imagine what that would have been like. You have all the wounded there, and there come I, sharing my fear with them, burdening them as it were, with my own fear. I don't think there would have been too many people who would have been able to cope with that sort of pressure. I don't know. I didn't talk to Bili about this. I'm not sure if Dr. Bosanac did. I'm not sure how they went about this. They would be better placed to give you that sort of answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Njavro, do you know if on the 18th, Dr. Bosanac and Mr. Bili were together throughout and do you know if they tried to get in touch with the Croatian government or anybody else? You were the hospital's chief surgeon after all. Were you informed about what people were talking about?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was only told that the hospital would be evacuated and I was told about the terms of this evacuation. Secondly I was let me say even far busier than they were. I was the surgeon in charge, after all, and I had to take charge of the wounded and of my staff. There were many things to be kept in mind, and I had to keep in mind all these things at the same time. I hardly had time for other concerns in addition to my work as a surgeon, treating the wounded and the sick.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You say that Dr. Bosanac talked to someone on the evening of the 18th and that she was told that an agreement had been reached, right?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure if that was at evening or in the afternoon. I don't remember that sort of thing. But I do remember what she told me, briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: That's fine, sir. Let's try to be brief on this subject. Do you remember if there was any -- if there were any messages being faxed between the hospital and the Croatian government on the 18th of November?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say with certainty. I know there was a phone link that was still operating, but I don't know about the fax link. I can't be certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: Did the hospital have a fax machine?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember if by any chance a request was faxed from the hospital to have a copy of the agreement forwarded to the hospital or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Were you informed in any way, were you told more about the terms of the agreement that had been reached, the agreement that Dr. Bosanac was told about on the afternoon or evening of the 18th?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't even see this treaty myself. I didn't go through it. I didn't read the treaty. I was told about the terms of the treaty by Dr. Bosanac, about the principal, salient features.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: On the 18th, Dr. Njavro, were you free to move about the streets of Vukovar, were you free to move about the hospital?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 18th I was still able to go around the hospital and see to it that the wounded got all the medical attention they required.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: On the 18th of November did you perhaps go to Dr. Bosanac's office? Do you remember going to her office on that day?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think she had a proper doctor's office. I think this was a room that she used for consultations. I think she kept her files in that room, and some of the patients' case histories were being kept there. I don't think she had a special room to herself. This was the room that one went to whenever there was something, an issue that needed raising with the doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Njavro, did you hear that on the 18th of November, 1991, a group, more specifically, a battalion of the so-called Croatian army surrendered at Mitnica, surrendered to the JNA, I mean?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I only learned about this when I was in Mitrovica, in prison. How else could I have known?

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you perhaps notice prior to the 18th of November, that there had been a largely increased influx of civilians to the Vukovar Hospital?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have been asked this sort of question before, and I clearly said that my family, too, was among them. There was this entire residential building, there were 20 flats there, and that was my building, that was where my family lived, and they all arrived at the hospital on that Sunday.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I suppose you talked to some of the people who were arriving at the hospital in those days?

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just one thing. Page 23, line 17, the date is missing. Sunday, the 17th. Or rather line 15, my apologies. Page 23, line 15. It should say, "Sunday, the 17th." There is no date. We can clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Njavro, let us not waste any time. When your family arrived on the 17th, when they arrived at the hospital, did you speak to any of the people arriving about what was going on outside the hospital?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke to my own family, and I learned about their experiences in the cellar. It was impossible to communicate at the time on account of the heavy shelling. They told me about their own experience. I realised that they were suffering from some health problems too, but I didn't have a chance to talk to anybody in particular. There were between 400 and 500 -- 450 people there who were wounded there, infirm, sick, elderly. I didn't really have time to go to anyone in particular to speak to people individually and ask them about their condition and their problems, but there were people who approached me and who told me about their experience, about what was going on in the cellars around town, that explosives were being chucked into cellars all over town, people were being killed, and that this was the principal reason that people started streaming into the Vukovar Hospital, in order to find safety there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Njavro, did you hear that on the 18th of November a large group of civilians were put up in Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 18th?

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, and I do know about these things, on the 19th --

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, please, sir.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that, then. That's your answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Njavro, what did you do on the 18th, after you returned to the basement? Were you still free to move about the hospital on the 18th?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 18th, on the 18th I think there was some complicated surgery that I had to perform on a young child, three years of age, I think. Who had sustained a serious wound during the shelling. The surgery required two or three hours of my time, and the conditions, obviously, were very difficult. I devoted some of my time and attention to that child. I had to make sure that the child would make it. I was free to go on later, although it was dark and I was using a candle to tour the hospital and visit all the wounded. I've spoken before about this to both the OTP and the Defence, haven't I? And then I walked back to that room just outside, but I think this was the only place, some bench or a chair where one could sit down for a while to get some rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: On the 18th at night, did you hear that there was still fighting going on around Vukovar? Did you hear sounds of explosions and people fighting?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already testified about this before. Maybe I wasn't able to really hear a lot of that at the time, but during the time I spent waiting for this to continue, I was thinking to myself all the time, there were explosions, sporadic ones. Maybe even there, but not near the hospital, yes. I can't say with certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned a person in your testimony, I mean Mr. Ante Aric. Do you know whether and why Ante Aric came to the Vukovar Hospital?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he came twice. I testified to the OTP, and also I testified --

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Njavro, please, let's not waste any time. It was a short question.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Allow me to clarify, because he came twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please go ahead, clarify.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: He came twice, because he was sent there by the Zagreb medical staff. They sent him to the Vukovar Hospital to help out. And the last time he came, let me try to remember, was sometime in August or early in September, 1991. He was a technician, a paramedic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please just repeat this, Mr. Njavro, for me? It's a bit unclear in the transcript. Who sent Mr. Aric to the Vukovar Hospital?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The main medical staff in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Njavro, we have a problem with the transcript. Can I please ask you to hold your breath for several seconds after I complete my question before you start answering?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What about the name of Josip Husar, Dr. Josip Husar does that mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Was he too a member of the main medical staff in Zagreb and was he the person who told Mr. Radic [as interpreted] to go to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if he was attached to the main medical staff, but I do know that Dr. Josip Husar used to work at the Vukovar Hospital and then he started his residency in Zagreb and he was off. I don't know if he was one of the people who decided to send Ante Aric to the Vukovar Hospital. I don't know. What I do know is that, as a native of Vukovar, Mr. Husar was very fond of Vukovar and he wanted to do something to help.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, correction for the transcript, page 26, line 1, it reads, "Radic," where, in fact, it should read "Aric", just so we avoid any confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this to clarify some information that I have. Is that Mr. Husar who later on was on the Rebro hospital in Zagreb, and then later in 1996 a scandal broke out when they -- involving negligent treatment of some three children who later on died?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Husar completed his surgical residency, and then he completed his further treatment abroad, I think in Germany. He was a specialist in paediatric cardiac treatment and it's true there was some affair that you told us. There is a medical association in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Njavro, we don't need to go into that, I just wanted to make sure that my information was correct. Filip Karaula, does the name mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know Filip Karaula prior to that. I heard of him back in Vukovar. As for his task, the task that he had during the aggression against Vukovar, I don't know that. All I can say is what I learned later on. However, during the attack on Vukovar I did not know what his task in defence was. As a native of Vukovar, I knew something about what was going on at Mitnica, but I didn't know his particular task at Mitnica. All I know is that he was a defender. But I don't know much about his specific task. I learned it later on, because I had contact with him subsequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Njavro, I'm not interested in what you learned subsequently. I'm only interested in the time period relevant for the indictment. When I asked you about Ante Aric, I omitted to ask you this: Did you see him on the 18th in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that Ante Aric was in the hospital on the 18th.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you think or are you sure of it, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't claim with certainty. I believe that he was in the hospital on the 18th, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Njavro, let us now turn to the 19th of November, 1991. Please tell us what happened on the morning of 19th of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can repeat to you what I already said.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: No need to repeat, please. I'm interested in learning who you first on the 19th in the morning, outside of the hospital personnel.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: A captain appeared, introduced himself. He said Captain Radic. He set some limits on my freedom of movement. The room that I already described to you was where I was supposed to stay for my safety. And then Ante Aric showed up, he warned him that it would be a good idea to take off his yellow ZNG boots, or else he wouldn't fare well. I think that that applied as well to the camouflage T-shirt that he wore under the white coat.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Can you remember what time it was, roughly?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Morning, I think around 8.00 or 9.00. And as I told you previously, I asked him about the events of the previous night in relation to the wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: No, no need to repeat that. We have that in the transcript. So this was around 8.00 or 9.00?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, roughly. In the morning hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What happened to you after 9.00 when captain told you that due to your safety?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A soldier remained by me, I was in the room.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Were you alone in that room?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: For a while. Until Ante Aric came, as I told you, and then the other --

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: And then there were the two of us there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Njavro, how long were you in that room by yourself before Mr. Aric arrived?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not long. After a while Aric was taken away. I don't know what time it was. But on that day, the 19th, Ante was led away.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Njavro, would you please focus on my questions? I have a line of questions, and I do not want anything extraneous to get in the way. So on the 19th, in the morning, the captain told you that due to your safety you were to stay in one room for reason of your safety, and then after a while Mr. Aric was brought to you?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: How long did you stay there together?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say. Less than an hour. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you remember when Ante Aric was led outside of that room on the 19th?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I can't claim with certainty. All I can say with certainty is that he was led away from that room.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: On the 19th?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, on the 19th.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: 19th of November, 1991, on that day, was he brought back to your room?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was brought back on the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What time?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think again in the morning hours. I'm not sure of the exact time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: From your previous evidence we learned that had on the 19th of November you were locked up in that room until about 7.00 p.m., and that at that time you left the room. I'd like to know how you learned that there were no soldiers outside of the room.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The door was constantly open. This is how the troops went in, went out, there was a lot of movement there. And in addition to that the soldier who was there had to take some breaks, so clearly he wasn't there the entire time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: All right. So on the 19th, in the evening, after 7.00 p.m. you left the room and went to tour the hospital; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but this tour of the hospital was rather a short one. Normally hospital rounds, except for surgical rounds, last longer, under normal circumstances. Surgical rounds don't take too long, unless there's a problem with the hospital. But -- or with the patient. But if everything is all right, surgeons make short rounds. However, on that day, under the circumstances, and in view of the fact that I was locked up in that room, I had to make a very quick round of the hospital, especially in view of what was taken place the previous night.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Njavro. So how long did it take for you to complete your round? Half an hour, an hour?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't say. I can't say either way. I don't think it would be proper for me to put a specific time on it. I was quite rushed with everything that was going on, so I couldn't keep track of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: All right. So you went back to this room?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You went back alone, nobody took you there?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: All right. And you stayed there until?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stayed in that room until, as far as I can remember, the entire night. We sat on the bench throughout the whole night, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You said, "We sat there." Who? You and?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Across there was a chair, so that some people who were still inside on the 19th, among them there a lot of people who had arrived from the town, so the place was crowded. People sat on top of each other, so some of them came.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Did you see on the 19th in the hospital Marin Vidic, Bili?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible, but I can't claim with certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: On the 19th of November did you see Vesna Bosanac in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the 19th Vesna Bosanac was in the hospital. And I think that she went to Negoslavci. She said, in passing, that she was going to Negoslavci to talk with Colonel, if I remember the rank accurately, I guess it was Colonel Mrksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether she went there?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, a driver who unfortunately is no longer alive, and I knew his family well, and the last name was Voloder, he took her there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have contact with Mrs. Bosanac on the 19th upon her return from Negoslavci, did she talk to you about the discussions she had there, and what you were supposed to do with the evacuation that had been agreed?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember now, but I think that Mrs. Bosanac did not return that night on the 19th from Negoslavci. I think that she remained either there in Negoslavci -- she remained there. But at any rate, she didn't spend the night at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: And when did you see her in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think on the 20th, early in the morning, at around 7.00. And then following that we had the assembly in the plaster room.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: All right. So when you saw her on the 20th in the morning, before the assembly in the plaster room, did you ask her about where she had spent the night, what was going on, what were the news, what was the course of negotiations?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I don't wish to be unpleasant, please don't take it the wrong way, but under those circumstances where our main concern was how to save the wounded, the sick, how to ensure that they stay alive, it was ridiculous for me to try to talk to her about the discussions she had had. Everything was happening quickly. She said that she was in Negoslavci, and talked to Mr. Mrksic, and as far as I remember, the evacuation was to unfold as had been agreed previously. As for additional details, I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Njavro, do you remember whether on the 19th of November, 1991, in the hospital in Vukovar you saw representatives of the International Red Cross, specifically Mr. Borsinger?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: On the 19th of November did you see Mr. Sljivancanin in the Vukovar Hospital?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that. However, I think that on the 19th, in the afternoon, they evacuated from the hospital all of those who had been there earlier assisting in the work, and also some of those who had arrived from the town, from the basements. We were told that everybody was to assemble outside of the hospital, that this was an order of Major Sljivancanin. But I think that I personally did not see him then.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So on the 19th you toured the hospital after 7.00 p.m. While you did that, did you see any JNA officers inside the hospital? Did you speak to any of them, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember that on the 19th, whether we spoke to them, except for the case in the morning, the incident with Captain Radic that I told you about.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Now, the preparations for the evacuation that you told us about, we heard in the meantime a lot of evidence from other witnesses about this. Do you know whether any defenders of Vukovar attempted to break through several days prior to the evacuation, on the 16th and 17th, and did you hear that those who did not succeed in this break-through came to the hospital, discarded their weapons, and put on civilian clothes? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't say anything about that. I know that Marko Mandic, who was a male nurse --

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Njavro, please answer my question. Do you know anything about this or not?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, would you please allow me to explain what I saw and experienced, because if I don't tell you that there were people, medical personnel from the hospital who went and came back, then I am not doing my job well. I'm not telling you about what I know. I know about the hospital staff. I don't know about other people, but I know about the hospital staff who attempted to leave the hospital, to leave Vukovar, and then they came back. Among them was Mr. Marko Mandic and his wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think it's time for the break, and then we can continue afterwards.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note that there is a lot of discussion going on among Defence teams and that creates a lot of disturbance for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I hope Defence counsel will note that last comment from the interpreters. Apparently there is audible discussion coming through on the microphones and interfering with their hearing of what is being asked and replied by the witness. We will -- Mr. Moore, are you wanting to raise something?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The next witness is P-021 being recalled. I think for my learned friend that they indicate that they might be approximately another half hour in cross-examination. Re-examination should not take a large amount of time. We thought that the cross-examination would be longer. The next witness we are obtaining, but there is an additional problem that Ms. Tuma, who dealt with that witness on the last occasion, has taken ill, and therefore I will be dealing with her. I have not had an opportunity of speaking to the witness, even if it is in short form. And I would like to have that opportunity at least to introduce myself and deal with one or two matters. It doesn't have to be done now, we can deal with this witness, but at the conclusion of this witness I would like a short adjournment of perhaps half an hour, so that I can deal with that point. I don't ask for a day's adjournment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: To minimise the interference with the progress, can I suggest a longer break now?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You could certainly suggest it. I regret to say that the witness is not here. I have asked for the witness to be here, and therefore if we use the time that we have to cross-examine and re-examine this witness, I would hope that the second break will arrive, and I can deal with 021 in that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Njavro, I spent the last break going through the transcript. There are two questions that I need to go back to, to clarify some issues. It's about the soldier that we spoke about, Ivan Zivkovic. He was on that convoy on the 19th of October, 1991. What I want to know is whether you remember Ivan Zivkovic, what were his injuries, who treated him when he arrived in the Vukovar Hospital?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember a man named Ivan Zivkovic, but I remember a lot of other names of wounded persons. I don't think I could specify his injuries though.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember Ivica Arbanas, does that name ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Who is he?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think Ivica Arbanas was a member of the ZNG.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Njavro, would it jog your memory in relation to Zivkovic, if you tried to remember this: Did Ivica Arbanas come to the hospital at the time and did he speak to Ivan Zivkovic, just to see if we're talking about the same person, sir?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't confirm. I can't say that I saw Ivica Arbanas talk to Ivan Zivkovic. I don't wish to repeat myself, but there was a large number of wounded persons streaming into the hospital, and it was difficult to keep track of who was talking to whom.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember if Ivica Arbanas came to the hospital during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did come a couple of times. Not very often, though. I'm sure about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps remember someone taking Ivan Zivkovic away from the hospital to be interviewed?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to go briefly into private session, if possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Njavro, you said a while ago you didn't remember seeing Mr. Sljivancanin at the hospital on the 19th of November, right?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but as I said --

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: No, please. Just answer my question briefly. During your testimony here Mr. Borovic in particular was showing you portions of your own book, the book that you wrote. The book entitled, "Heads Bowed, Hands Behind Backs." And it appears that your book contains not only your own experiences, but also the allegations of some other people. Specifically on page 141 I found a portion where you claim that on the 19th of November Major Sljivancanin arrived at the hospital and addressed you. I quote: "Doctor, I have a special reason for wanting to talk to you." Does that jog your memory?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course it does, and it's not the first time that I have to say this. And not only here. It's possible that I may be wrong about some dates. There were things like that happening, and the editor changed some dates as he saw fit. I can now say that this was on the 20th, the morning of the 20th, following the meeting in the plaster room. That's when he told me this. I remember his words clearly and I stand by my previous statement. This was on the 20th of November, 1991. The morning of the 20th.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: He had a special reason for talking to you, so did he end up talking to you or not?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you talk to Mr. Sljivancanin at all?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What about before that?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before that he gave a speech, a monologue in the plaster room.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about you and Mr. Sljivancanin, any contact or communication, just the two of you?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No except for what I have just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Are you saying it wasn't you who told Mr. Sljivancanin about members of the ZNG in disguise who were in the hospital at the time?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think there were any, so I couldn't have told him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What about the JNA people at the hospital on the 19th or on the 20th, because you say there might be some confusion about the dates. Did you tell any of them that Mile Dedakovic was in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: How could I possibly have told anyone anything like this? Everybody knew that Mile Dedakovic had long left Vukovar. He left early in October, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Who told you about that? Who informed you about Mile Dedakovic leaving Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, counsel, there was permanent, ongoing telephone communication with Zagreb and with Vinkovci. One knew this sort of thing. Dr. Bosanac was sending out warnings and appeals to a number of international institutions. She spoke to Zagreb, she spoke to our command. She spoke to the health ministry's Main Staff, and they were touring the front lines. She knew that Mile Dedakovic had left Vukovar, and she knew where he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you tell anyone that Marin Vidic, Bili, was in the hospital at the time?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who I possibly could have said this to. Somebody may have seen him at the hospital. He wasn't hiding, he was openly moving about the hospital. There would have been no need for me to tell anyone that Marin Vidic, Bili, or Dr. Bosanac were there. It was normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you tell anyone on those days, the 19th or the 20th of November, about the fact that some persons were shamming wounds and that their false wounds were dressed and bandaged just so they could pass themselves off as wounded. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, there had been a promise to Dr. Bosanac from the Main Staff in Zagreb that there would be an evacuation of the wounded, sick, civilians, and medical staff. If that indeed was the case, and why shouldn't have been, given the situation at Vukovar at the time, what was eventually done was the usual thing you do when you have to provide transport for people who are seriously wounded. Plaster-casts are applied, their wounds are bandaged, and nothing outside this was done. Only the usual, established practice in such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, if I tell you that Dr. Bosanac, while testifying here, even yesterday, said that on the 19th of November, 1991, Mr. Sljivancanin talked to her in the hospital, and that he arrived together with Mr. Borsinger, and that she had lists of wounded persons in the hospital and that she gave one copy to Mr. Borsinger, and that Mr. Sljivancanin took all the remaining copies, and that this was in the afternoon on the 19th of November. Would you at least allow for the possibility that this was, in fact, the case?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why would I doubt anything that Dr. Bosanac claims? But you know where I was at the time, in which room.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Let's go back to the return of Mr. Aric on the morning of the 20th. What time was it?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact time Mr. Aric was returned. I'm not sure if it was in the morning or in the afternoon. What I do remember is that there was this military vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I will be moving on to that later on.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the time. I don't remember the exact time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you talk to him when he returned to that room?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said what I've already mentioned. If you want me to, I can repeat that for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: No need, thank you. Do you remember Dr. Ivezic?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think he was a major, or a colonel, but I wasn't sure about his rank. He took over the command of the hospital, as far as I could tell, based on his behaviour. I think he was a surgeon from Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see him at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What was he wearing?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: A military uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Were the European monitors there by then by any chance? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to Dr. Ivezic did you see any other officers arriving with him, people who were doctors?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember one particular anaesthesiologist who said he was from the military medical academy from Belgrade. He set off with me. That was on the 20th. Our duty was to record all the remaining wounded in the hospital, to make a list. I was taking down their names, and he followed. The wounded were asked what sort of treatment they wished to receive, and where.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember if these doctors, Dr. Ivezic and the other doctors who arrived with him, interviewed any doctors of the Vukovar Hospital such as yourself, Dr. Bosanac? Did they ask to have any documents?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't interview me, they didn't talk to me, but they did talk to a number of Serb doctors who remained at the hospital throughout these horrors of war that we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can we please have Exhibit 338 placed on our screens? This is a photograph, and the number is 0036-6995. Mr. Njavro, when the photograph comes up, please have a look and tell us what you see. Do you recognise anybody in the photograph, where was it taken? Exhibit 338, please. Yes, this set is the one, the photograph number is 0036-6995. Yes, that's right. Can you see the photograph, Dr. Njavro?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nothing. I can see a globe on my screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: So it hasn't come up on your screen yet?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Is this Dr. Ivezic?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a man of a certain age, but whether this is him, I can't say. I can't say for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Where was the photograph made?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The photograph was taken in the so-called nuclear shelter, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember when this photograph could have been taken, since we see the man in the JNA uniform on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say. I can't even say that the man on this picture is wearing a JNA uniform. It's not clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Well, I will not insist on this in that case. You said that your wife and mother-in-law came to the hospital on the 17th?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: On the 20th of November did any members of the JNA or Mr. Sljivancanin ask, request that you and them be transported to Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't see him after the speech in the plaster room, and the instance where he told me where to stay. After that I had no further contact with Major Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: All right. So you saw him in the plaster room in the morning?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: How was he dressed?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, this is quite a sensitive time that we are describing now, but I think that he wore a camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did he have any rank insignia?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that he did, I think that there was an inscription, a sort of a badge somewhere on the side, whether he also had something on his epaulets, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the inscription on that badge or plaque, was there his name or something else?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember what was written. I think he had a plaque, I probably did read it at the time, but I can't remember any longer.
