utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did he have any other insignia, any other symbol on his uniform that you registered?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But I did register his appearance, his face, and this is something I will remember for as long as I live.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let us now go back to the 18th, to your first encounter. Did you know at the time the name of the major who talked to you outside of the hospital and to Mr. Borsinger?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, at the time I didn't know that this was Major Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, tell us, when did you learn that, and when did you link this?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The moment it was said, and when Mr. Borsinger was told this, it was then that we learned that there was a commander. Earlier Mrs. Bosanac spoke to Mr. Mrksic on the phone, and as I've told you, they reached a certain agreement, and it was then said that he was the commander of the entire operation against Vukovar, the attack on Vukovar. So the logical question that emerged was who is this new person that suddenly surfaced.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Njavro, I have to interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please let me conclude.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: No, I will let you conclude everything that is relevant for my questions. When did you learn that the person that you talked to on the 18th was called Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned that on the 19th in the morning. And I think that I already gave evidence about this when I described the arrival of Captain Radic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Who told you on the 20th in the morning that there would be a meeting of medical personnel?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure who said that we had to assemble, pursuant to the orders of Major Sljivancanin. All medical personnel was to assemble in the plaster room.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember when you arrived, did you arrive on your own, or were you accompanied by someone?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were a lot of us medical personnel who could fit into that room. That's not a very large room, but nevertheless it was full. There were a lot of us employed at the hospital, medical staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember what time it was when the meeting started?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure, but it was in the morning, could have been 8.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know how long the meeting lasted for?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's hard to say. Not long. I don't think it was longer than one hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Did any of the doctors that you mentioned, such as Dr. Ivezic, anybody else, were they also present with Sljivancanin at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say. As I have told you, there were a lot of us medical personnel in the room and it would be hard to say who else was there. I mean the officers from the JNA, I simply don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that on the 20th some other JNA officers arrived later on, they inspected the hospital, talked to some doctors, and so on?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have told you, I know Dr. Ivezic. I mentioned him. There was also an anaesthesiologist from Belgrade. Now, whether there were some other doctors there, it's possible. I simply don't remember. I don't remember whether they conducted any interviews, went to see the wounded, and so on. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: A witness told us something here, and I will now put a question in relation to that to you. Did the Vukovar Hospital, among its equipment, have a refrigerator where human organs were kept?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Whoever said something like this had to be, and I have to use strong language here, is a person who was out of his senses, who had no more contact with his brain.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: So you had nothing of the sort in your hospital?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Naturally we had a pathology department where they might have kept temporarily people who died in order to perform an autopsy on them. Unless you have in mind the blood, because blood, after all, is a human organ, and we did have some blood supplies for transfusion. So in some sense, yes, it is a human organ, and we did have that. But we had that only up to a point, and then we ran out of blood supplies.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: That's precisely what I want to ask you. When did the blood supplies run out?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Blood supplies, that was toward the end, 10 to 15 days before the end. But you should ask the transfusion specialist who was in charge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: All right. You mentioned the pathology department where autopsies were performed. How long -- for how long did they perform autopsies?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, they did not do any autopsies in the most difficult times. That room was hit by shells, so they really did not have any working conditions, and the pathologist felt it was unsafe, and I don't think that under those circumstances he could have done the job.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Does that mean that on the 20th, in the morning, there were not corpses in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether somebody died in the meantime. I can't say that with certainty. We always had seriously ill patients and the wounded who were moribund, so it could be that somebody died. I, as a surgeon, for many reasons, was not allowed to have any contact with such individuals. In the vicinity there was a building where we took corpses of those who had died in the hospital, but also corpses of those who had been killed somewhere else in the city, and then their bodies were taken there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Njavro, I have to ask you this: I'm now referring only to the 20th, the 20th of November. On that day there was no refrigerator where blood supplies were kept, there was no pathology department. There was no section of the building where you could have kept human organs. Is this a correct conclusion that I'm drawing, just say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: How could we have had that? There was no electrical supply. Even if we did have a refrigerator, we would not have been able to use it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You said that whoever said that he saw something like that on the 20th of November, a refrigerator, where human organs were kept, and that there was a stench coming out of there because there was no electricity, you say that whoever said that was out of his mind?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I used a figurative description. It was impossible to keep any human organs because in order to preserve them, one needs a transplant specialists, and this is advanced medicine, and we had no such experts at the time in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Dr. Njavro, I know that, please don't misunderstand me, this is something that we heard from a witness, and I'm not going to repeat this witness's name. On that day in the plaster room, was Dr. Neda Striber present?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. She's a petite woman, and perhaps she was there, but I didn't notice her.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether Binazija Kolesar was there?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember Mara Bucko, was she present?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: She's a nurse, I know who she is; I think she was there, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether Dr. Bosanac was there?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, she was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What about Dr. Ivankovic?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Stanojevic?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember Mirko, I don't remember him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: This speech that Mr. Sljivancanin gave, as you told us, the monologue, did he mention in it that the doctors and medical personnel could remain in the hospital working?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember this portion of the speech any longer. I just remember the colourful words that were used, namely that the army was there, that he was in charge of them, that there were different uniforms there and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: All right. You told us all about that. Let's now clarify about Marin Vidic. Did you see him at the hospital on the 20th?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that he was there on the 20th, but I'm not fully certain. I can't be adamant about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What about Stipe Pole and Josip Gazo were they at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I most likely -- or rather had I seen him, I would have known that they were there. But I didn't see them. Josip Gazo could not have been there, if we have in mind the same person. There are several person the with that last name. If we have the same person in mind, then he had left Vukovar long before that. Three months prior to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What about Stipe Pole?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was there until the end. As I said to Mr. Borovic, when the MUP building was demolished, he moved to a building across from my apartment flat, and that building belonged to Vupik, to the agricultural concern.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Njavro, you said in your statement that on the 20th you spoke to an Italian man, a representative of the ICRC?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what time it was and did this take place inside the hospital or outside?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Inside the hospital. He was a short-ish man of dark complexion. I spoke some Italian, was able to understand some, and he said that he was an ICRC representative. When I went around with the anaesthesiologist from the military medical academy in Belgrade when we were recording the names of those who remained, and you should know that at the time the hospital was half vacant, a lot of people had already gone. And -- and this anaesthesiologist told me to write in two copies, one copy was given to the Italian. I thought he was an Italian, that was my impression, I didn't ask him. But he was the ICRC representative. And the other copy was given to the anaesthesiologist.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Njavro, you spoke to us about that?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I'm interested in the meeting in the plaster room. After it concluded, how long after that did the ICRC representative arrive?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was in the afternoon, it could have been 2.00 or 3.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What did you do after the meeting in the plaster room? You said it began at about 8.00 and went on for about an hour, so from 9.00 on?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's what Captain Radic had said previously and what Major Sljivancanin now repeated to me. I stayed in that room, I had a view of the emergency entrance. I saw what was going on there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you help with the evacuation?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was unable to. However, at about 2.00 or 3.00 in the afternoon there were some wounded left, and another fellow doctor was taking them to a truck. His name was Tomislav Vlahovic, a surgeon from Zagreb. He was in charge of that truck. We placed the wounded on that truck, and that was the last bit that I helped with, but that was all.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: At the time you spoke to the Italian from the Red Cross, do you remember seeing Mr. Borsinger there?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember seeing any European monitors?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Njavro, what about the name of Sasa Jovic, does that mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Sasa.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think Sasa Jovic was a young soldier, perhaps he was even a JNA sergeant who had been seriously wounded, and I treated this young man at the hospital. If that's the person that I have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the very person, Sasa Jovic. Do you perhaps know under what circumstances he was wounded and what the injuries were that he sustained?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the circumstances, but I know that he was abandoned and that it was the ZNG who brought limb to the hospital. We took charge of him, we treated him successfully, I hope. I hope that his health is now good, that he is a healthy young man, not too young anymore, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know if he was enjoying any form of special protection while at the Vukovar Hospital?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: If there is a war going on, then human relations tend to work in a different way, tensions are created which can lead to clashes. It is for this reason that we took Sasa Jovic and Srdjan Miljkovic, another JNA soldier, he had sustained a serious wound to his lungs. We had a special room for those two, they were kept separate from the rest just in order to prevent any incidents from occurring. On the 20th, or on the 19th, the JNA took charge of them when they came and I have no idea what happened to them later.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: This brings to mind the testimony of a witness here. Do you remember on the 19th of November whether there was a foreign TV crew visiting the hospital? Do you remember any cameramen or anything like that on the 19th?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It strikes me as possible, but I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What happened after 3.00 p.m.? What happened to you on the 20th?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was getting dark because this was winter-time. A military vehicle drove up, may have been a jeep, but I'm not certain. And a lady appeared, a lady officer. She entered the hospital. She had arrived with Captain Radic. Ante Aric and I were taken away. He had been brought back to the hospital earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: On the 20th you are in this meeting in the plaster room. What happens -- what's happening to Ante Aric? When did you see him again?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember when I saw him again, but I'm certain that I saw him when we were inside that military vehicle. We were together inside that vehicle, there was this lady officer driving us back to the Vukovar barracks, back to Sajmiste.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: How long did you stay there, how long did you stay in the barracks?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: For about an hour. It was pitch dark already, and Dr. Bosanac joined us in the Vukovar barracks at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: So where did they take you and was it the same vehicle that they used?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they took us, but I'm not certain if it was the same vehicle or an APC, but they took us to Negoslavci. Aric got off the APC in Negoslavci, and stayed there. Dr. Bosanac and I were put in that same APC and taken to Sid. We spent some time in Sid and we were again joined by Ante Aric. After this they took us in a paddy-wagon of sorts. With benches inside, wooden benches on either side. And an opening with curtains that the driver and the passenger could open and close. So there we are, leaving Sid for Belgrade. We read the road signs, the sign posts, and we realise that we are on our way to Belgrade. Sometime past midnight, it's really difficult to say, I wasn't paying much attention to that, to be quite honest, but it was the middle of the night. We were taken to Topcider, or to Dedinje. We eventually arrived outside a barracks, I think it was the one at Topcider, but I can't be certain. We parked right there, the driver and the escort got off, some military officers, I don't know about their ranks because the curtain was closed. They walked up to the barracks gate, they spent some time there talking, and we were waiting to see what would become of us. After some time they returned, they turned around, they turned the vehicle around and we were driven back from Belgrade to Sremska Mitrovica. It wasn't before 3.00 or 4.00 a.m. That we reached Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Fine. Let me ask you this: Sid, Belgrade and Sremska Mitrovica, Dr. Bosanac, Aric and you all together, right?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Is there a soldier guarding you? You are sitting in the back, shut up. Was there a soldier with you?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there was a soldier in the front seat, there was the driver and there was somebody else too, some security or escort.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You talked about arriving in Sremska Mitrovica and what happened there. You were even offered the option of working there as a doctor, of setting up an infirmary or something. But you asked to be assigned another doctor to give you a hand with that, right?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: After some days in Mitrovica, after some days of interviews, as we were being taken to one of these interviews, we met somebody who introduced himself as the chief medical officer in Sremska Mitrovica. I think he was a major or a colonel. His first name was Gojko. I forget his last name. I know what sort of a doctor he was. He was a specialist for pulmonary disease.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the speakers please talk one at a time?

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Does the name Sadika Bilus mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Two or three days later there were a lot of wounded with their wounds festering on account of neglect. There was a -- there were some cases of sepsis, and I asked around to see if there were any other doctors there. So that they could give me a hand with things that I wasn't so good at.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Njavro, please let's not waste time? Do you know Dr. Bilus from the Vukovar Hospital --

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Was at the meeting in the plaster-room?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note. Could the speakers be asked to speak one at a time? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we seem to be having a problem with the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The transcript seems to be having a problem with you, Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're quite right there, Your Honour. We'll try to deal with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Let us simplify matters, Dr. Njavro. You knew Sadika Bilus from the Vukovar Hospital, right?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What was she doing at the Vukovar Hospital?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: She was a specialist for internal diseases.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see her on the 20th of November, 1991, at the Vukovar Hospital?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember seeing her at Sremska Mitrovica? I imagine that was the 21st or 22nd or the 23rd, whatever?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was several days after the rest of us had arrived in the camp, at Mitrovica that I saw her. Several days later, as I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: How were your relations with Miss or Mrs. Bilus?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mrs. Bilus. She was a very good specialist. However, back at the hospital when there were so many things to keep in mind, and to see to, all the wounded, all the sick, she was sometimes filming stuff without even asking for permission. I think she should have asked for permission to be allowed to film people, to film the wounded. We told her that was not a good thing to film people, the wounded and the sick, without having obtained permission. We cautioned her that this might be unlawful, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know why she did that?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever talk to her about this?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but there were suspicions that some things happened that weren't supposed to happen without anybody meaning to do this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What exactly do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean that persons who were seriously wounded or had suffered a massacre ended up on TV screens without their permission or approval.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Who could have aired this footage?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. She probably gave these films, these tapes to someone for them to be aired.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You saw her in Mitrovica, right?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What did she look like?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Like a lady. She was all dressed up in her best finery, unlike the rest of us. We didn't look much, we hardly even washed. We couldn't stand close to each other because the smell was that bad.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I will quote something from your book, and you tell me if the description fits Mrs. Bilus: "A lady walked down the prison stairs all dressed up wearing make-up with a perfect hair-do in a new costume wearing high-heels." Is that what you wrote at the time?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I wrote. She told me she'd been to Negoslavci before she arrived in Mitrovica. I hadn't had a proper wash in quite some time. So this was a chance to pay some more attention to my personal hygiene. That's what it looked like at the time. I may have exaggerated a little bit, but she certainly was different from us. She was much neater.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Was she involved in the work of the war infirmary or surgery?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ask her how she came to look that way, how she obtained that privilege?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I asked her where she came to Mitrovica, she said she'd been placed in a solitary cell, that there was a bathroom there, that she could wash and dress properly, comb her hair. Which is less than you could say of the rest of us, because our conditions were somewhat different. We couldn't even dream of anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I understand that. That's precisely why I'm asking the question. Did you ask her how she got to be granted that privilege?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may as well have, but I don't remember the question or the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Another quote, another portion from your book. She told you that the reason for her enjoying this sort of privilege was that, as you say in your book, "She said that she had told them everything she knew." That's one thing. You go on to say: "Likewise the prison administration or the camp administration were familiar with the fact that we had been in touch all the time with Vukovar defence commanders." And then further down the tapes that she recorded, the tapes that you're talking about, ended up in the hands of the enemy, and it was based on these tapes that the enemy could identify a lot of people whom they found to be of interest and who were locked up in prison somewhere. It was because of that tape, and because there were no records that they couldn't prove that anyone was a member of the guards of the reserve forces or the MUP. We were quite surprised, even shocked to hear her story. Just because none of us had any documents that might have jeopardised the safety of any of the prisoners in Sremska Mitrovica." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this is quite simple. When this was said, the bit that just read out, and there were some 100 of us in the room, I'm not going to speak of the conditions, I don't think the Trial Chamber is interested in that. But I know that after she left in the following days when they went to be questioned, some individuals came back with serious injuries. Therefore, it was logical to conclude what you just read out, what is written there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: While in Mitrovica, did you see any other persons we mentioned here during your evidence? Did you see Mr. Vidic?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Bosanac?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not even her. Even though there were women who came to seek medical treatment from me and they said that Dr. Bosanac was with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Dr. Njavro, we're now going to turn to a technical issue, medical documentation created in the hospital. Can you tell us something about that, how was a wounded patient admitted? What kind of information was entered, and into what kind of books? Did each ward in the hospital have their registration book and were these records compared in terms of the initial diagnosis and the final one?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm going to repeat what I said previously. We had two registration books. The first one is where the personal particulars were recorded, and then medical history information was recorded, and then the third type of information was how the illness or the accident occurred, and where. That was the first book. The second book, in cases where we had seriously wounded persons, was the surgical book, and this is something that each surgical team had in their surgery rooms. This is the book where they would normally enter a preliminary diagnosis and then a final one. They would also briefly record what was established and done in the course of this surgery, who operated on the patient, who assisted during the operation, what type anesthesia was given and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What about log-books for anaesthesiologists, did they have one?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They recorded anesthesia given to a patient, and then when a patient was about to be discharged, you know prior to that we had medical charts where everything would be recorded; the course of the treatment, any problems and so on. This would also be recorded in the medical chart. Anaesthesiologists also had their recording books. Precisely what was administered to a patient, under whose instructions and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: All right. So the information concerning the admittance of a patient, a patient who needed a surgical procedure and therefore needed anaesthesia, were these records reconciled, did anybody compare them to see the records from the admittance and then the records from surgical procedure and reconcile them anaesthesia information?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: If anybody was administered anaesthesia, it is unlikely that that wasn't recorded. However, in the first book, in the book of admittance, anybody could look into that book, even the physicians who were on -- undergoing their residency treatment. They would write in a diagnosis, for example, they would say that something was going on with the abdomen, and there was a minor wound there. Looking in the book, this physician could conclude that the treatment was not a very long one or a very detailed one. However, if one took a more detailed look, you know, they could come to the conclusion that this required serious treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I am afraid that we misunderstood each other. Mr. Njavro, all I'm interested in is this: Was it possible for a patient who was admitted and who required a surgical procedure to be registered in the book of admittance without being registered in the book of anaesthesia?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if it involved light injuries. For example, local anaesthesia could have been administered without it being recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Outside of these cases, if total anaesthesia was administered, what then?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that case it had to be recorded fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: All right. We spoke about your departure from the Vukovar Hospital and then we spoke about how you were set free later on. Did you ever come across any documents from the Vukovar Hospital from this period of time?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in a sense that a spoke to some people. Let me remind the Trial Chamber of something that I spoke about earlier. When you asked me about the 19th of October, when the convoy of Medecins sans Frontieres took some seriously wounded people outside of Vukovar, all of them had either a discharge letter on them, or some other documentation. Please let me conclude, because this is in a way an answer to your question. And yes, this is the type of documentation that I did come across later on in Zagreb and in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. I'm speaking of the documentation that remained in the Vukovar Hospital. Not the ones that the evacuated patients took with them.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The documentation that remained in the Vukovar Hospital, which, as I said, was taken away and ended up at the military medical academy in Belgrade, according to the information that we have, I know nothing about that documentation. I never saw it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You, as a doctor, if somebody were to ask for some kind of a letter, a certificate, about treatment received, would you have been able to issue such kind of a certificate, a letter, without having the documentation at your disposal?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would have been able to do that in relation to many of the patients. I used to have a great memory. It used to be the case, not any longer. So up to 19 --

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no, I'm just asking, would you have been able to do that?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in some cases, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Njavro, what were your relations with Dr. Ivankovic like?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe they were quite proper. I have respect for Dr. Ivankovic, I consider him to be a very good surgeon, he practiced his profession very well. I have nothing else to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You said that proceedings were instituted against you in Belgrade and that Dr. Ivankovic came as a witness to testify against you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear what the witness said. The speakers overlapped.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: If I were to tell you that Mr. Ivankovic was heard before the military court?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what he stated, Mr. Ivankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, page 63 of the transcript, line 11, do not reflect the answer that the witness gave. Dr. Njavro said, "No." And if needed, I can put the question again. The question pertained to whether Mr. Ivankovic appeared as a witness in the trial. Mr. Njavro said, "No."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I did not see him in Belgrade. We're speaking of Belgrade now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether he testified at all in the court in Belgrade in the case against you?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have no information to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: From 1992 until nowadays, have you ever seen Dr. Ivankovic?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I saw Dr. Ivankovic when negotiations were held about peaceful reintegration. I think that it was then that we met, we needed to discuss how to fit the existing medical system into the medical system of Croatia. And naturally we also met once we returned to the Vukovar Hospital when everybody who had been expelled from Vukovar was enabled to work there again. Incidentally, I have a statement given by Mr. Ivankovic, I don't know whether he changed his opinion in the meantime, but in this statement he expressed his opinion about me. And it was a positive one, just like my opinion of him. So I'm glad that at least at a professional level we seem to understand each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but as far as I remember, there was something negative concerning a plot of land that was given to him?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that wasn't my comment. You know that doctors seem to be -- seem to have a lot of solidarity. Seem to have a lot of solidarity among them, they seem to generally respect each other. What you stated was the position of the citizens of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Njavro, did you have any contact with the security service of the defence ministry of Croatia concerning the events in Vukovar? Did you have any contact with them before you came to testify here?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Categorically, no. I never, never had any contact either with officials from the Ministry of Defence with even from the Ministry of Defence or from any other organs. We never discussed the testimony given here, nothing was discussed about the trial held here. I can assure you of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any contact with the Security Service of the defence ministry about the events in Vukovar, excluding testimony given here, did you have any contact with them?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I had any contact with the Ministry of Defence. As the Chamber knows, and as I spoke in my introduction, I was health minister, and I had other business to take care of.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: So can I conclude that you never talked to anyone from the Security Service of the Ministry of Defence of Croatia about the events in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never. I never had any talks with them. And I have to say that I'm surprised about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: So am I. I have just one more question, and we have reached the end, the final end, Mr. Njavro. Do you remember how many statements in total you gave about the events in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's hard to say. I wouldn't be able to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I don't want to break any more promises, but let me try to put it this way: Did you ever testify before any court in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bulatovic. Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, yesterday, late in the evening, we received an additional statement related to the witness we heard today. This is pursuant to Rule 60(A)(ii) [as interpreted] we received it only in English, but that's not a problem. Transcript reads Rule 68, it should be Rule 66(A)(ii), although maybe it should have been submitted under Rule 68, at least that is the defence position. The name of the witness is Radomir Dejanovic. Legal interests of my client require that I put additional questions to this witness pertaining to this statement that was disclosed to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. Moore?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, I do. The first thing is as follows: That statement was only obtained last week, so therefore it's not a case of the Defence having a document delayed in any way. The second relates to the fact that this witness should not be cross-examined on the document, and I'm loathe to actually reply in the presence of the doctor. I don't know if it's possible for the reply to be in the absence of the doctor. Although I suspect the name, having been given, clearly indicates what the topic is about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, I don't know that Mr. Borovic intended to actually be cross-examining on the document. I would understand him to be indicating that the statement has given rise to issues which he needs now to explore with this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I would be surprised if that was the case. Because I know the statement, and I know the nature of the statement. That's why I made sure that he got it before this witness gave his evidence. As I say, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: But he only got it a few days ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: He got it yesterday. Because, as I say, we only obtained the statement, we only spoke to the witness, I think it was last week we managed to locate that witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, on the one hand you say you object to him cross-examining arising from the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: On the other hand you say you made sure he got the statement before this witness gave his evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes. I made sure that he got the statement because it is relevant to cross-examination that was -- that Mr. Borovic made on the last occasion, and a challenge that he put. Now, the witness did -- had said -- well, if needs be, I will explain it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We do not know what's in the statement, and we not know the issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You and Mr. Borovic do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, we do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: But it appears to the Chamber that there is a fundamental inconsistency between you seeing a need to ensure that Mr. Borovic had the statement before this witness continued with his evidence, and you now saying that he shouldn't have an opportunity to cross-examine, because of this new information provided to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: No, I understand entirely the Court's logic. But I'm submitting that it does necessarily follow. The statement that was obtained related to an individual that Dr. Njavro had said that Mr. Radic had requested -- Radic had apparently requested to see a doctor at the hospital. And Dr. Njavro gave a name. He was cross-examined on it, and said that Mr. Radic did not know that doctor, and that the educational background was different, that the doctor that Radic himself was educated in Sarajevo, whereas the doctor was not. So the information certainly relates to earlier cross-examination, but in my submission there is nothing in the document that would allow Mr. Borovic to cross-examine this witness. Because the witness has given evidence saying, "I believe he said the following name." And that was all. And the cross-examination was, "Well, that name is unknown to Radic, and the criteria that you apply are different. He was not educated at that place, he was educated elsewhere." He was given this statement, under Rule 68, the correct procedure for this statement and this witness is either for the Prosecution to admit it, which I am willing to do, or for the witness to be called to say, "I do not know Radic and I have never known Radic." This witness, Dr. Njavro, cannot answer any of the material in the statement. There is nothing there for him. He doesn't know the details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic, you have leave to cross-examine. But the need will be for you to be relevant to this witness. And it may be, if Mr. Moore is correct, that there won't be much that you can put. We leave that to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I'll try to be as brief as possible, needless to say. May I just remind the Chamber that I cross-examined Mr. Njavro on this additional witness, he provided several pages of answers in reference to this name. It wasn't a single reference, there were several. And also there was this KOS captain who was interviewing doctors and then what was said was the KOS captain particularly wanted to know about a rather young colleague, Radomir Dejanovic a physician.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that -- a general practitioner -- do you remember that, that I showed you that.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: This was on the following page, Your Honours, 1679, and the date is the 15th of November, 2005. This is the intro. I was asking a number of questions, and the witness Njavro said as follows: "As far as I remember, Captain Radic asked me about Radomir Dejanovic, what my opinion of him was." And then: "I know he commented on their relationship because apparently they were fellow students at the military academy and the medical school back then." And now we're getting to the point. Do you know that Radomir Dejanovic was born in 1956?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. Never thought to ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. I then told you what our Defence position was, that he could not have been there, that he was not a JNA counter-intelligence service captain, I also told you that he had studied in Sarajevo, which you can tell if you look at the information contained in the indictment, there was no way they could have studied together in Belgrade. What I am about to tell you now is this: Based on the statement, paragraph 5 of the statement, it says that Radomir Dejanovic started university in 1975. Another thing I wish to tell you is that Captain Radic was born in 1962. Therefore, he was but a young boy at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I object to the way the question is being put. It's not a question, it's giving evidence. And that's exactly what I have been trying to indicate. All this doctor has said is, I thought it was, and my learned friend is only now giving evidence in relation to the topic. And that's wholly inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the president, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: At the moment, I don't see a way that you can usefully put this sort of question to the witness. It would seem to me that your position, as advanced, most by taking advantage of what has been indicated by Mr. Moore, that he would agree to this statement being tendered as an exhibit so that it then becomes evidence that that is the position. I'm not sure how the witness can help you when he has told you what he recalls of the person. It may be the right person or a wrong person. He can't help you with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will do my best after all, this is very important for me. This is evidence for me about what the counter-intelligence captain talked to that doctor about, but this could not have about Captain Radic, this is a case of mistaken identity. Now, how can I prove is this? I will rephrase the question If I tell the witness that Radic was still a child.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Doesn't that statement help you to establish that they're two different people?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine, Your Honours. Can I just ask one more question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You can ask any relevant question arising from the statement. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a highly relevant question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did you watch a movie called, "100 days of Vukovar" on Croatian TV several times?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure about several times, but I did see that movie, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did you see a particular piece of footage showing Captain Radic allegedly saying this: "Vukovar must fall tonight."

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have any further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Finally, Your Honours, you have been very kind and I thank you for that. I seek that Dejanovic's statement be admitted into evidence based on the confirmation that I received from my learned friends from the OTP today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be Exhibit Number 350.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Moore, looking at the time, our tape is just on the verge of running out. I think a break will be necessary, unless you are going to be very, very confined.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I would have thought I would be no more than 10 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I don't think we've got 10 minutes on the tape. And you need a longer period now to see the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Could Your Honour say a quarter past 1.00?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could you live with 10 minutes past 1.00, Mr. Moore?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Time is becoming of the essence. 10 minutes past 1.00 we will resume.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Doctor, you've told us about seeing an argument between Sljivancanin, as you believed him to be, and Borsinger, the international -- the Red Cross representative. Do you remember giving evidence about that?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Were you able to hear Mr. Moore's last question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'll ask the question again, if I may. You have told us about an argument between Sljivancanin and Borsinger that you saw at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: How many times did you see them together when one considers that period?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 18th, as I said, outside the hospital it was in the early afternoon. I did not see Mr. Borsinger and Mr. Sljivancanin meeting at any time after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So the answer is, you saw them together once; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And you described it as an argument. Now, you have told us that it is possible that you may be wrong in dates on occasion. That's right, I think, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If you look at the sequence of events, the succession of events, if the JNA and the paramilitaries entered Vukovar on the 18th, and laid siege to the hospital, and everything I told you about what was going on inside the hospital, that could have been on the 18th, the afternoon and the evening of the 18th, the 19th, or the 20th. If you --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. Now, can I deal with the argument that you say was between Borsinger and Sljivancanin, you have heard, because it was put to you by Mr. Bulatovic, that we have had evidence from Dr. Bosanac that the meeting actually was not the 18th, but the 19th. Now, is it possible that it might have been the 19th?

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic. Just pause a moment, please, Doctor. Yes, Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, at no time during my cross-examination did I suggest to Mr. Njavro that the meeting took place on the 18th. I'm not sure where Mr. Moore got this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I never said the 18th. I thought I said the 19th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The transcript holds you to the 18th on three occasions. Maybe it was a misspeaking on your part, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, I will repeat it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Line 17 --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- 18 and 19, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Or not 19. Sorry, line 15 is the first one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, actually, if you look at line 24, now is it possible the meeting might have been on the 19th. What Dr. Njavro has said, it was the 18th. Mr. Bulatovic reminded the witness about a meeting on the 19th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If you are content with your question as it is there, there will be no ruling against its propriety by the Chamber, Mr. Moore, despite the objection. No, Mr. Lukic, you've had the objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, not objection, Your Honour. Not objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that problem is with the transcript because Mr. Moore asked a meeting, and translation, what we received and witness received is "sastanak."

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, thank you very much. And what does that mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My understanding was that Mr. Moore was referring to the encounter between Borsinger and Mr. Sljivancanin outside the hospital. That was my understanding, so is that perhaps a possibility? I think there is some confusion involving the words "encounter," and "meeting." I think it's a matter of interpretation, and I think that is what is causing the confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You told us that the meeting with Borsinger and Sljivancanin was on the 18th. And you've told us there was only one that you remember. And Mr. Bulatovic reminded you that Dr. Bosanac said that meeting was not the 18th, but the 19th. And I'm asking you, bearing in mind the rely you gave, is it possible the meeting was on the 19th and not the 18th, as you said?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The encounter between Mr. Nicholas Borsinger and Mr. Veselin Sljivancanin occurred on the 18th, the first one. The 18th of November, 1991, outside the hospital in the afternoon. On the 19th Dr. Bosanac told me, and this was a well-known fact, that the men, the staff who were inside the hospital who had come up from the cellar to seek salvation inside the hospital, that they, that is what Dr. Bosanac told me, that doctor -- that Mr. Sljivancanin, and that he was taking such people away. On the 19th I personally did not encounter Mr. Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I think you may have misunderstood what was said to you. I'll repeat it again. You have told us there was one meeting by -- or between Borsinger and Sljivancanin. You believe that to be the 18th of November. But you have heard from Mr. Bulatovic that Dr. Bosanac took the view that the meeting was not the 18th, it was the 19th. And when you were asked about that you said, "Why should I dispute what Dr. Bosanac said?" So what I'm trying to do is to clarify, please, whether it is possible that she is right and you may be wrong about the date. That's all I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I categorically claim that I heard what I said on the 18th outside the hospital entrance. And I told you about the way they spoke to each other, Borsinger and Sljivancanin. It was on the early afternoon of the 18th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'll move on to another topic, if I may?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Just before you do, is there something further, Mr. Bulatovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I felt it best to try and get that resolved by I heard your objection. Very well, carry on, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we deal, then, please, with Marko Mandic? Now, you know that name because you've already given evidence about it; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, a question was asked by Mr. Bulatovic, and it was as follows, "Dr. Njavro, did you hear that on the 18th of Nova large group of civilians were put up in Velepromet?" Answer by yourself: "On the 18th?" Question: "Yes." Answer, and this is what you said: "As far as I know, and I do know about these things on the 18th" -- and then you were stopped. Now, what were you going to say about the things you knew about in relation to Velepromet on the 19th? Do you understand the question?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the 18th -- what I said occurred on the 19th and not on the 18th most of the men from the hospital who had arrived from cellars were taken away among other people, one of the persons we talked about, Marko Mandic. There were a number of ambulance drivers, too; certain security officers from the hospital. I think there were two or three police officers, I can give you their names, if you like. One of them was Tomislav Hegedus, and the other was Branimir Lukenda and, as I said, some of the ambulance drivers too, and we don't know what became of them, what fate they ultimately met. What we do know is that they were taken to Velepromet, I'm talking about the 19th of November, about the 19th of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And Marko Mandic, was he at the hospital around the time of the fall of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And can you tell us what happened to Marko Mandic?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Marko Mandic was a paramedic. He was a plaster technician for limb injuries. He was very, very good at his job. He was in the hospital on the 19th with this group that I've mentioned, including those others who had arrived from across the town to seek safety inside the hospital, so he was taken away, together with that group.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: If we are talking about this group of men that you say were taken to Velepromet, are you able to estimate how many men were taken to Velepromet on the 19th from the hospital?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's difficult for me to give you a figure, but it was a substantial amount. As I said, those from the cellars, though, somehow had managed to survive all the shelling, all the destruction and all the horror. Everything about that. So, those who arrived at the hospital at one point in time, between the evening of the 17th and the 18th, there must have been nearly 2.000 people, if my assessment is correct. How many of them were taken away, I only know about the hospital staff and the health workers. How many others who were in the -- on the ground floor of the hospital, how many of those were taken away, I can't even give you a ballpark figure, except for those I have already mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But that is not what I am asking. I'm asking specifically about the group of men, and you described people like Tomislav Hegedus. I'm asking about that group being taken away on the 19th, and I want you to concentrate on the 19th. Now, are you able to give an estimate of the number of men taken away on the 19th to Velepromet? Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Prosecutor, I can only tell you what I know. What I know about the hospital, and the people who were taken away. A large group of men were taken away, that much is certain. I don't know the exact figure, but I know about the hospital employees. However, there were many other men there. And they, too, were taken to Velepromet. This is at Sajmiste, the warehouses belonging to that company. A large number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When you refer to police officers, how many police officers were taken on the 19th, approximately?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for police officers, I think a man named Baketa was taken away, Tomislav Hegedus was also taken away, Branko Lukenda was taken away. I'm not sure about anyone else. I can't remember, but those were the people in charge of the hospital security. They made sure that there were no incidents inside or outside the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I want to deal with male hospital staff that you believe were taken away on the 19th, and please focus on the day. On the 19th, to Velepromet, can you tell us the names of the hospital staff taken away on that day, please? If you don't know, do say.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of the drivers, Marko, Vlaho, another man named Vlaho, another man, Miroslav, not Marko, Azasanin, Mihajlo Zera. The drivers. The ambulance drivers. Hospital employees, Dragan Gavric. These are some of those that -- that I can now remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And of the names that you have given, do you know what happened to those individuals? Have you ever seen them again?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never again. None of the ambulance drivers I've just mentioned or the police officers for that matter, or the hospital staff. I've never seen anyone again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I have no further re-examination. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Doctor, I once again thank you for coming to The Hague and for the assistance that you have given. You will be pleased to know that should be the end of your evidence, and you are now free to return to your other interests. Thank you very much. The court officer will assist you outside.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to be efficient, and ask for some guidance while we're waiting for the next witness. It has to do with the following: Yesterday we received a written request from the Prosecution pertaining to two witnesses that Mr. Moore said several days ago he was planning to call. If you will remember, upon hearing that from Mr. Moore, I said that we would like to submit a written filing, pertaining to that. What is important for us is that we be able to do this within eight days. Mr. Moore's submission is three pages long. We have a problem that you are not aware of, and I will let you know about it now. The statement of the proposed witness, Florence Hartman was disclosed to us in English. And it has three pages of text. It is not too long. We did not receive it in B/C/S, even though the Prosecution ought to have disclosed to us in B/C/S, but they did not and we will read it to our clients ourselves. What I need to make you aware of are the attachments that came with the statement. In order for us to be able to state our position concerning this, we received 10 pages in French, handwritten pages, this was one of the attachments. Then we received an article in French, then we received another article in French that she mentions in her statement, I think it's an article from Le Monde. Then we received 30 pages of other notes she made, handwritten in French, a total of about 30 pages. Mr. Moore can confirm this. Then another article in French from another newspaper. Also, a portion of a book, I can't read it out in French, it has to do with Milosevic, and then parts of the book entitled: "Milosevic: Diagonal of a Madman and Diagonal of a Laufer." Both 10 pages long. Now we are faced with a task that should have been made easier for us by the Prosecution. We have to acquaint ourselves with the documents in order to make our submission. We received this in one of the official languages of the Tribunal, and I don't know whether Mr. Moore speaks French or not, but he had to familiarise himself with these documents as well, especially the notes made by the witness. So I am now asking that we be allowed to make a written submission, and I don't know what are the intentions of Mr. Moore, whether he wants to tender these documents into evidence pursuant to Rule 66(A)(ii), if he intends to tender them in at all. We received this just two days ago, only in English, not in the language of the accused, and this was disclosed to us on the 30th of March. I wanted to make you aware of that so that you understand why we're asking for eight days to write our written submission. So this pertains to Witness Hartman and Witness Aric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: With regard to Florence Hartman, the statement says here is in three pages, it's a straightforward statement, and it's being translated in B/C/S to assist my learned friends. I can't imagine that there's any difficult in reading the statement, and I see Mr. Lukic saying no. With regard to the attachments or appendixes, Hartman's statement really breaks into two parts. One is a discussion with Major Sljivancanin, and the second relates to the discovery of the grave at Ovcara where we submit that she will be able to say that the grave was located on or about the 18th or 19th of October, 1992. And as a consequence of that, she, being a journalist, that article was subsequently published in Le Monde and associated newspapers. So the newspapers themselves are being translated also. The trouble of course that arises is it takes time. But the actual nub of the statement is that she discovers the grave on the 18th and 19th of October. We have asked for the translation and it is being done as quickly as possible. I'm a little -- well, it's not my business to say that I'm surprised but the fact of the matter is the statement goes to those two issues, one is notice and one is a discussion, and the material will come through when the translation department manage to conclude their work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: When it is anticipated that the witness will be called?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If leave is granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: If leave is granted we were hoping because there is a problem actually next week and I will explain it now that it has arisen. We have a witness who was to give evidence from a foreign jurisdiction. Because of the nature of the terrain, there have been difficulties setting up a satellite link, and the government and the police force of that country are trying to change the location to a major city. I think, as matters stand, we need of course the registry to be there, and we had intended it to occur before Easter. I think that that will not be able to be done until after Easter. We were hoping that we could have dealt with the matter of Hartman perhaps sometime next week if there had been a decision. I don't mean that in any discourteous way. But it was one of the reserve witnesses that we had because she's here in the building and can be brought in at short notice. We have another witness where we made application for protective measures, which was granted yesterday. We have attempted to locate that witness, I'm not going to go into the details of it, and that is proving to be difficult. We are still hoping that the witness will be available on Monday, in substitute for the grave digger. But as it stands at this time, we are trying to locate that person. What I had anticipated was that next week, the new witness with protective measures for Monday and Tuesday, and then the 92 bis material to be on Wednesday because I felt it was inappropriate to start a new witness on the Wednesday, bearing in mind there was a public holiday coming up on the Friday with a long break. So the 92 bis material is going to be dealt with by Ms. Tuma. So with regard to Hartman, the situation is, it just depends when the translation department concludes. The one good thing is that she's in the building and could always be re-called if there is any untoward that appears.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Anything in reply, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The current position of Mr. Moore is shocking. I find it shocking. And I will tell you why. If the Prosecutor intends to call the witness next week, the witness about whom we were informed just a few days ago, or rather we received the material just a few days ago, I don't know how the Defence is supposed to make investigations. The investigations needed for cross-examination. We need to contact our investigators. Your Honours, the Prosecution intends to call another 30 or 40 witnesses. And because the Prosecution does not have ready witnesses for next week that's not reason enough to call somebody for whom we are not prepared. In general we oppose the calling of new witnesses. We need at least one month to conduct our investigations for these two witnesses, about whom we were informed just recently. Let me tell you something else. In a meeting in January Mr. Moore did tell us indeed that he intended to call Mr. Aric. We were disclosed the statement of Mr. Aric from the year of 2000. At the meeting Mr. Moore also told us that he was going to take a new statement from Mr. Aric when he is called here. So far we have received only the 2000 statement. We expect to receive new material that we will then investigate through our investigators. I said that this involved the notes of Mrs. Hartman, which are completely illegible for us. If you will remember just how difficult was to read Mr. Kypr's notes and how important they were for the trial. The submission that the Prosecution gave us about the proposed testimony of Mr. [As interpreted] Hartman will indicate that our fears are quite legitimate. We have to conduct our own investigation. I don't see how we are supposed to cross-examine the witness, if she is to come, if we receive these documents so late. We need to translate them and then conduct our investigations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Any response, briefly, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, there is. We had two witnesses, one a grave digger and one that we have asked for special measures which we hoped to call in time, which would conclude next week. It was not our intention to call Aric or Hartman next week. As I have said, that they are almost substitute witnesses, because of the difficulties that we have had with regard to the electronic contact, which has been going since, I believe, January, we've had I think, three dates so far. And with regard to Aric, we can call Aric at any time. The difficulty we have is, one witness we are having difficulty to locate, and the second relates to electronic problems. I understand my learned friend's concern about cross-examining Hartman, but I am trying to fill the court diary as best I can. And there is nothing approaching 30 to 40 witnesses to be called by the Prosecution. I would estimate probably between 12 and 14. I would anticipate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think the Defence observation is well placed upon the lists we presently have, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, my learned friend also knows that we have said that we are cutting down the military witnesses significantly. The problem is perfectly straightforward, we are not sure, given the nature and conduct of the Defence, exactly the form of the cross-examination. And I am very loathe to say I am not going to call a witness, a military witness, if -- without knowing exactly what the nature of the cross-examination is. I'm trying to be as careful as I can in an important case, and I do not wish to say that I'm not going call someone, and then find the nature of the cross-examination is going to be dealt with by that witness. I gave an estimate that I thought that mid-May, and I don't think I'll be far away with regard to that date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: In the view of the Chamber it would be inappropriate in the circumstances if either of the two contemplated witnesses were called next week unless it is the case, in respect of Aric, that the evidence to be given is that which was in the statement provided some months ago. If there is to be a new statement and different evidence, it would not be appropriate to call the witness next week. Just to keep the scales even, let it be clear the Defence cannot expect a month to investigate any additional witness. We must now adjourn and resume tomorrow at 2.15 [sic]. Could I indicate -- sorry it's 9.00 tomorrow. Can I indicate that on Friday morning two new judges are being sworn in at 9.00, so that we must be delayed until 9.45, I expect, before we can start. That's on Friday. Tomorrow morning at 9.00 we resume.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 6th day of April, 2006, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.52 p.m.,
